sections.h2: La Paz County at a glance
sections.html:
Out on Arizona's western edge, La Paz County has a small tax base and a lot of open space: 4,514 square miles and 16,557 residents at the 2020 count. Parker is the seat and biggest town, with Quartzsite the only other incorporated town, and the Colorado River Indian Reservation takes up the western side.

The census found 13,457 housing units in 2020. Of those, 45.2% stood vacant, and 71.8% of occupied homes were occupied by their owners. Mobile homes are common, and the Assessor's office keeps the records for them. Ownership is updated from Motor Vehicle Division title records, and the roll cannot change until a new title is issued. Until then, the previous owner keeps receiving the notice of value and the tax bill. If you are selling a mobile home, check that the title has actually been transferred.

Property tax here is a two-office job. The La Paz County Assessor handles value, ownership, parcel maps, exemptions, mobile homes and business personal property. The La Paz County Treasurer sends the bills and takes the payments. Because the Assessor sets no rates, mails no bills and neither collects nor refunds money, you call the Treasurer about an amount due and the Assessor about a value.

  • Treasurer: 1112 Joshua Avenue, Suite 203, Parker, AZ 85344. Hours are Monday through Thursday, 7:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m., with Fridays closed.
  • Assessor: 1112 Joshua Avenue, Suite 204, Parker, AZ 85344, phone 928-669-6165.
  • Recorder: 928-669-6136, for deeds and recording fee questions.

Deed details come to the Assessor from the Recorder, and permit details come from La Paz County Community Development, the Town of Parker and the Town of Quartzsite. A room added or a roof lost without a permit can still surface on the roll later, so put your permit paperwork in the sale file.

Two payments cover the year: October 1 and March 1 (A.R.S. 42-18052). The Treasurer counts a payment late after 6:00 p.m. on the delinquency date, and postmarked payments are accepted. Expect a minimum payment of $10 or 10% of the tax due, whichever is greater.

DateWhat happens
October 1First half comes due, after bills are mailed in September
Early November, 6:00 p.m.First half is delinquent
December 31, 2026Final day to pay the full year without interest
March 1, 2027Second half comes due
May 4, 2027, 6:00 p.m.Second half is delinquent

An unpaid first half is already accruing interest. Clearing the entire year before December 31 ends it, which a December seller can arrange at the closing table (A.R.S. 42-18053).

Once a bill is delinquent, the county charges 16% a year without compounding, and even a partial month is charged in full (A.R.S. 42-18053). The Treasurer applies that 16% in monthly steps from the first of the month until payment.

Interest is off the table in three cases:

  • A mistake by the assessor or treasurer produced the delinquency.
  • The whole year is paid in full by the end of December in that tax year.
  • A mortgage or deed of trust was released the previous year, in which case the treasurer may waive interest and penalties one time for the property if the supervisors agree.

For a sale, ask the Treasurer for a payoff that holds through your closing date. Parcel search and card payments are on the Treasurer's website. Paying by Visa debit adds $4.00, a credit card adds 2.55%, and the jurisdiction code you give over the phone is 1312.

If the notice looks wrong, you have 60 days from its mailing to petition the County Assessor. A.R.S. 42-16051 sets that limit and treats the postmark as your filing date. Owners of record get a notice each year, and only the full cash value or the property class may be challenged.

Your petition should say what you think full cash value is and back it with real evidence. State law names three approaches: income, market and cost. For the market approach, you need a comparable property or the sale of the property in question. A recent arm's-length purchase of your own house is the best evidence you can bring.

Note that limited property value is a different figure. Proposition 117 holds its growth to 5% a year, with exceptions found in A.R.S. Title 42, Chapter 13, Article 7. Bills run on limited value, so a rise in full cash value does not always lift your tax by the same amount.

The Assessor administers two programs, and its staff can quote the current income and value limits. Phone 928-669-6165 before you list.

  • The exemption for widows, widowers and totally disabled persons age 17 or over. Applicants must live in Arizona, fit within income rules, and stay below an indexed assessed-value limit. A physician must certify that a disability is total and permanent.
  • Senior Property Valuation Protection, known as the senior freeze, which holds limited property value steady for three years. The owner must be 65 when applying, live in the home as a primary Arizona residence, and meet income rules.

A value can jump when a buyer takes over a home whose prior owner held a senior freeze, so a buyer should expect a first notice of value that looks higher than the seller's. Owners of short-term rentals should also look at the rental registration form on the Assessor's page and the state's online lodging marketplace registration.

sections.h2: Questions to settle before you list
sections.html:
A little groundwork keeps the sale on schedule. With the Assessor, confirm that the owner of record is the person signing the deed, and ask whether any exemption or senior freeze is attached to the parcel, because a buyer's first notice of value may look different from yours. With the Treasurer, ask what is open for the current year and for any older years, and have the payoff dated for the day you plan to close. With the Recorder, ask what the filing will cost.

Hold on to anything that proves permits were pulled for work on the house, and for a mobile home, make sure the title has the right name on it. Hand the same set of figures to your title company so everyone works from one number. Sellers who live elsewhere should start with a phone call to the offices in Parker.

Heirs often find a tax bill addressed to someone who has died. Before you list, find out who is the owner of record and make sure the Assessor has your mailing address, so you do not miss a notice of value and the 60-day window that follows it. Ask the Treasurer for the balance and for any earlier years that remain open. If the house is a mobile home, check that the Motor Vehicle Division title has moved into your name, because the roll cannot change before that. Then give all of it to the title company at the start, not the end.

The tax lien attaches on January 1 of the tax year (A.R.S. 42-17153). Only state liens and tax liens from other years outrank it. It lasts until taxes, penalties, charges and interest are paid, a buyer takes title at a tax sale, or a certificate of removal and abatement is issued. Expect the buyer's title company to want the current year and any earlier years cleared out of your proceeds.

Owing tax is routine at a sale as long as the numbers are clear. Follow this order:

  1. Request a payoff from the Treasurer dated for your closing.
  2. Check the owner of record with the Assessor.
  3. Hand both figures to the title company.
  4. Sign the deed with its sworn affidavit of property value under A.R.S. 11-1133. The recorder must refuse the deed without it unless an exemption is noted.

For recording requirements and the current fee schedule, call the Recorder at 928-669-6136. With a cash buyer there is no lender timeline, so the county payoff is often the one open item left.

faqs.q: What happens if I do not pay the first half of my La Paz County tax?
faqs.a: It goes delinquent and 16% annual interest starts building. Settling the whole year by December 31, 2026 stops more interest, under A.R.S. 42-18053.

faqs.q: Where do I pay La Paz County property tax?
faqs.a: Send or bring payment to the County Treasurer, 1112 Joshua Avenue, Suite 203, Parker, Arizona 85344, or use the website or phone. Do not plan on a Friday visit, since the office keeps Monday to Thursday hours, 7:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m. Cards cost extra: $4.00 on Visa debit and 2.55% on credit.

faqs.q: How long do I have to appeal my La Paz County notice of value?
faqs.a: You get sixty days, counted from the day the Assessor mailed it. The petition goes to the County Assessor, and under A.R.S. 42-16051 your postmark is the filing date.

faqs.q: Does La Paz County have a senior property tax freeze?
faqs.a: Yes. Senior Property Valuation Protection freezes limited property value for three years. The owner must be 65 at application, use the home as a primary Arizona residence, and meet income limits. Call the Assessor at 928-669-6165 for the form and current limits.

faqs.q: Can I sell a La Paz County house that still has tax due?
faqs.a: Yes. Closing pays the lien from your proceeds. Ask the Treasurer for a payoff for your closing date, because interest runs monthly on delinquent amounts, and pass it to the title company.
